screens.title: Publish-Subscribe Pattern in ROS
screens.narratorSegment: The publish-subscribe pattern is a one-to-many, asynchronous messaging model where a publisher sends messages to a named topic and subscribers receive them without knowledge of who sent them. In ROS this decoupling is essential: sensors, planners, and controllers interact through topics rather than direct links. The Master coordinates discovery by recording which nodes publish and which nodes subscribe; it does not forward messages. After registration the publisher and subscriber establish direct TCP connections and exchange messages, which keeps the runtime efficient and scalable. A useful mental model is a radio station: the station broadcasts, any number of radios can tune in, and the station doesn't need to track each radio. A common misconception is thinking the Master is in the message path; that is not correct and leads to confusion when diagnosing latency. Another practical point is that topics are asynchronous, so subscribers may receive messages at unpredictable times depending on network and processing load. For example, a camera might stream at thirty frames per second while a processing node subscribes but can only handle five per second; without proper queue sizing the processing node will either lag behind or drop messages. Reflect: which robot data should be broadcast to many consumers and which should be handled point-to-point?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Publish-subscribe decouples senders and receivers; the Master handles discovery while nodes exchange messages directly over TCP.

content.html:
Core Concept

Publish-Subscribe Pattern

A publisher sends messages to a topic; subscribers receive them without needing to know the publisher. The Master only registers participants and helps them discover each other.

  • • One-to-many and asynchronous communication.
  • • Master coordinates discovery; it does not forward messages.
  • • Subscribers connect directly to publishers via TCP after discovery.
Key Takeaway

Decoupling via topics makes it easy to add or remove consumers without changing the publisher code.

Radio Station Analogy
Publisher = Radio Station
Broadcasts messages without tracking listeners.
Subscriber = Radio
Tunes to the topic and receives messages independently.
Master = Operator
Connects the station and radios but is not on-air.
Misconception
The Master is not a relay. Messages flow directly after discovery.
Check your understanding
Which data streams on your robot are best as topics because many nodes need them, and which should be services or actions instead?

screens.title: How Topics Are Named
screens.narratorSegment: Topics have names like file paths: slashes separate namespaces, and a leading slash indicates a global name. For example /robot/cmd_vel and /camera/image_raw are distinct topics. Names without a leading slash are relative to the node's namespace, which makes it easier to reuse nodes across robots by changing namespaces. Following a hierarchical naming convention helps avoid collisions when multiple robots or sensors are present, and it clarifies intent. A typical convention is to put robot-specific prefixes like /robot1 or /robot2 so tools and launch files can control which robot a node operates on. A common pitfall is assuming a node publishes to the same topic regardless of its namespace; when you move a node under a different namespace its relative topics change. Use absolute names when you want a node to always publish to the same bus, and use relative names when you intend to remap or reuse the node under different namespaces. Think about which naming style will make your system easy to inspect with rostopic list and less error-prone when copying nodes between robots. How Topics Are Named means use hierarchical names and decide between global and relative names to control reuse and prevent collisions.. In practical terms, namespaces, global vs relative names, and common conventions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Topic naming
keyIdea.text: Use hierarchical names and decide between global and relative names to control reuse and prevent collisions.

content.html:
Definition

Topic names are hierarchical

Use slashes to separate namespaces. A leading slash makes a name global; without it a name is relative to the node namespace.

Example: /robot1/cmd_vel vs /robot2/cmd_vel — two separate buses for two robots.
Tip: Use relative names in reusable nodes so they can be remapped with launch files.
Pitfall: Forgetting namespaces can cause subtle bugs when similar nodes run for different robots.
Why it matters

Clear naming prevents topic collisions and makes rostopic list output easier to navigate.

Namespace Examples
Global name
/camera/image_raw — always the same global bus.
Relative name
camera/image_raw — resolved under the node's namespace at runtime.
Remapping
Remap relative names in launch files to change topic targets without code edits.
Check your understanding
If you place two identical sensor nodes under /robot1 and /robot2 namespaces, how will rostopic list show their topics?

screens.title: ROS Message Types and rosmsg
screens.narratorSegment: ROS messages are typed data structures defined in. msg files and compiled into language-specific classes or structs. Typical standard types include std_msgs/String for text, std_msgs/Int64 for integers, geometry_msgs/Twist for velocity commands, and sensor_msgs/Image for camera data. Knowing the structure of a message is essential before publishing or subscribing: you need to know which fields to set or read. Use rosmsg show followed by the message type to print its fields. For example rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist reveals linear and angular Vector3 fields with x, y, z components. For many mobile robots only linear. x and angular. z are used, which simplifies your publisher and subscriber code. A common mistake is assuming a Twist message contains only two numbers; the message actually contains nested Vector3 fields, and you must populate the correct components. Practically, inspect a type with rosmsg before writing code and choose standard message types when possible to maximize interoperability with existing tools and nodes. Definition

ROS Message Types

Messages are typed; fields and nested structures determine what data you send. Use standard message types when available.

Common types: std_msgs/String, std_msgs/Int64, geometry_msgs/Twist, sensor_msgs/Image, sensor_msgs/LaserScan.
Inspect: rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist to reveal linear and angular Vector3 fields.
Tip: For 2D mobile robots typically only linear.x and angular.z are used.
rosmsg example
geometry_msgs/Vector3 linear
  float64 x
  float64 y
  float64 z
geometry_msgs/Vector3 angular
  float64 x
  float64 y
  float64 z
Concrete example
Using Twist for velocity commands
Set linear.x to forward speed and angular.z to rotation rate; leave other components zero for planar robots.
Common misconception
Assuming message types are loosely structured. In fact, fields are explicit; sending malformed data will not match expected fields.
Key Takeaway

Always inspect message fields and choose the most specific standard type available.

keyIdea.title: Python pattern
keyIdea.text: Initialize node, create rospy.Publisher, use rospy.Rate, loop while not rospy.is_shutdown, publish messages and sleep on the rate.

content.html:
Process

Python publisher walkthrough

This example publishes a String to /robot_news at 2 Hz using rospy.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rospy.init_node('robot_news_radio', anonymous=True)
    pub = rospy.Publisher('/robot_news', String, queue_size=10)

    rate = rospy.Rate(2)  # 2 Hz = 2 messages per second

    while not rospy.is_shutdown():
        msg = String()
        msg.data = "Hello from the Robot News Radio!"
        pub.publish(msg)
        rospy.loginfo("Published: %s", msg.data)
        rate.sleep()
Key elements explained
  • rospy.init_node creates the node and registers it with the Master.
  • rospy.Publisher defines topic name, message type, and queue_size.
  • rospy.Rate keeps a steady publish frequency and adjusts for loop time.
  • rospy.is_shutdown ensures the loop exits on Ctrl+C or ROS shutdown.
Concrete example
Run the script and watch rostopic echo /robot_news print messages at 2 Hz.
Common mistake
Using time.sleep instead of rospy.Rate can ignore shutdown requests and produce unstable rates.

screens.title: Publisher Loop Details: Rate, Queue, and Shutdown
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson focuses on three loop behaviors that determine the reliability of your publisher: publishing rate, queue_size buffering, and clean shutdown. First, the rate: use rospy. Rate or ros::Rate to keep the frequency stable. These objects sleep for the remaining loop time, so short workloads still match the target frequency. Second, queue_size controls how many outgoing messages are buffered if subscribers fall behind. A queue_size of 10 keeps the most recent ten messages; older ones are dropped. For high-rate sensors where only fresh data matters, choose a small queue so your subscriber always processes the latest sample. For command logs where every command matters, increase the queue or consider a service or action. Third, clean shutdown: check rospy. is_shutdown or ros::ok inside the loop so your node stops gracefully on Ctrl+C. A frequent debugging step is to run rostopic hz to confirm the publish frequency and rostopic echo to inspect payloads. When messages are dropped due to a full queue, you will see gaps in subscriber processing or stale data; monitoring hz and bw helps you spot these problems quickly.

keyIdea.title: Loop reliability
keyIdea.text: Use Rate objects to maintain frequency, choose queue_size based on freshness needs, and honor shutdown signals for graceful exits.

content.html:
Process Flow

Publisher loop: rate, queue_size, shutdown

Maintain a stable rate
rospy.Rate and ros::Rate compensate for loop processing time to keep the target frequency.
Buffering with queue_size
If a subscriber is slow, publisher buffers up to queue_size messages and drops older ones when full.
Clean shutdown
Check rospy.is_shutdown or ros::ok to exit loops gracefully on interruption.
Example scenarios
High-rate camera: publish at 30 Hz but subscriber handles 5 Hz. Use queue_size of 1 to avoid stale processing.
Command logs: if every command must be delivered, increase queue_size or use a different mechanism so no commands are lost.
Check

Use rostopic hz to confirm publish rate and rostopic echo to observe dropped or delayed messages.

keyIdea.text: Use ros::init, ros::NodeHandle, nh.advertise<T>(), ros::Rate, and ros::ok to publish messages in a compiled node.

content.html:
Process

C++ publisher walkthrough

This example shows a minimal nh.advertise publisher that sends std_msgs::String at 2 Hz.

#include <ros/ros.h>
#include <std_msgs/String.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    ros::init(argc, argv, "robot_news_radio");
    ros::NodeHandle nh;

    ros::Publisher pub = nh.advertise<std_msgs::String>("/robot_news", 10);
    ros::Rate rate(2);  // 2 Hz

    while (ros::ok()) {
        std_msgs::String msg;
        msg.data = "Hello from the Robot News Radio!";
        pub.publish(msg);
        ROS_INFO("Published: %s", msg.data.c_str());
        rate.sleep();
    }

    return 0;
}
Key differences
  • Type parameter: advertise<T> uses the message type as a template.
  • ros::ok vs rospy.is_shutdown: ros::ok returns false when ROS requests shutdown.
  • Compilation: C++ nodes are compiled; ensure proper includes and linking against message packages.
Concrete example
Build and run the executable, then use rostopic echo /robot_news to confirm messages appear at two hertz.
Common mistake
Forgetting to add the correct message package to CMakeLists and package.xml will cause compile errors, not runtime errors.

screens.title: How the ROS Master Enables Connections
screens.narratorSegment: The ROS Master is often misunderstood. Its role is discovery: it keeps a registry of nodes and the topics they publish or subscribe to. When a subscriber registers interest in a topic, the Master responds with a list of publisher endpoints and the subscriber establishes direct connections to those endpoints. This direct TCP connection carries the message traffic without going through the Master, which avoids a single bottleneck and increases throughput. Think of the Master as a phone operator that hands out numbers but does not stay on the line. This design also means that once nodes find each other, network topology and firewall rules can affect message flow—if nodes cannot open direct connections, messages will not be delivered even though the Master knows about them. A practical troubleshooting step is to check rostopic info for a topic to see which nodes the Master knows are publishing, and then confirm direct connections at the OS level if you suspect network issues. How the ROS Master Enables Connections means master provides discovery only; after that publisher and subscriber communicate directly via tcp, avoiding centralized message forwarding.. In practical terms, discovery vs forwarding and the direct tcp connection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Master role
keyIdea.text: Master provides discovery only; after that publisher and subscriber communicate directly via TCP, avoiding centralized message forwarding.

content.html:
Architecture

Master: discovery, not relay

Master stores registration information and returns publisher endpoints to subscribers so they can connect directly.

• Master reduces coupling but is not on the message path.
• After discovery, nodes open direct TCP connections for efficient streaming.
• Network or firewall issues can block these connections even if the Master knows about publishers.
Why check

Use rostopic info to see what the Master knows and then verify direct connections if messages are not flowing.

Troubleshooting steps
  1. Run rostopic info /topic to see publishers the Master knows about.
  2. Use rostopic echo to confirm messages arrive at a subscriber.
  3. If messages do not arrive, check network connectivity and firewall rules preventing direct TCP links.
Analogy reminder
The Master hands out addresses like a phone operator; it does not carry the conversation itself.

rostopic command-line toolbox

Show active topics visible to the Master.

screens.title: Queue Behavior and Stale Data
screens.narratorSegment: Queue behavior determines whether subscribers see every message or only recent ones. When a publisher sends messages faster than a subscriber can process, messages accumulate in a queue up to queue_size. If the queue becomes full, older messages are dropped so that the most recent messages are preserved. For time-sensitive data like camera frames, dropping old frames is often desirable because processing an old frame produces stale results; using a small queue or a queue_size of one ensures subscribers process the latest data. For command sequences where each command must be handled, dropping messages is not acceptable and you should either increase the queue or use a different communication mechanism such as services or actions that provide acknowledgements. A practical way to observe queue effects is to run a publisher at a known high rate, subscribe with a slow consumer, and use rostopic echo to see gaps in timestamps. Remember: choosing queue_size is a design decision balancing freshness, memory, and delivery guarantees. Queue Behavior and Stale Data means a publisher's queue_size holds recent messages; when full, older messages are dropped so subscribers process more recent data instead of stale data.. In practical terms, how message queues affect subscriber processing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Queue semantics
keyIdea.text: A publisher's queue_size holds recent messages; when full, older messages are dropped so subscribers process more recent data instead of stale data.

content.html:
Definition

Queue behavior and stale data

If producers are faster than consumers, messages buffer up to queue_size and older messages are dropped when full.

Small queue: keeps only the most recent messages; best for sensors where freshness matters.
Large queue: buffers more messages; useful if every message must be delivered and processed later.
Observation: gaps in rostopic echo timestamps indicate dropped or delayed processing.
Key Takeaway

Choose queue_size based on whether freshness or guaranteed delivery is the priority for the data stream.

Concrete scenario
Camera stream
Publish at 30 Hz, process at 5 Hz; use queue_size = 1 to avoid processing old frames.
Command queue
If commands must be delivered, increase the queue or use services to ensure no commands are dropped.
Check
Run rostopic hz and rostopic echo while varying queue_size to see the effect on delivery and timing.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas. Finally, queue_size determines buffering behavior and trading freshness against guaranteed delivery. Keep these points in mind when you design topic interfaces or debug live robot systems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll demystify the publish-subscribe pattern and how ROS implements it with topics and publishers. You will see why topics act like named message buses, how the Master helps nodes discover each other, and why messages are typed. We'll use practical examples: a simple Python publisher that sends text, a C++ publisher that sends the same message, and command-line tools that let you inspect live traffic. Understanding this model matters because it is the backbone of how sensors, planners, and controllers exchange data on a robot. For instance, a camera publishes images and many different nodes can subscribe without the camera knowing them. A common confusion is thinking the Master forwards every message; it does not. The Master only registers who publishes and who subscribes, and then nodes connect directly. Throughout the lesson you'll run small publishers at fixed rates, examine message fields, and use rostopic to confirm rates and contents. By the end, you'll be able to pick the right message type and publish at a stable rate, and you will know how to check for dropped or stale data.

Over the next lesson you will develop four concrete competencies that let you integrate nodes using topics. First, you will explain the publish-subscribe pattern and how topics implement it in ROS. That includes being able to describe the Master’s role in discovery and why nodes connect directly afterward. Second, you will write a Python publisher that sends messages at a fixed rate and know how to use rospy. Rate and rospy. is_shutdown to exit cleanly. Third, you will write a C++ publisher that advertises a topic and uses ros::Rate and ros::ok for clean loops. Fourth, you will use rostopic command-line tools to list topics, echo messages, and check publishing rates. Each objective focuses on a practical demonstration: running a publisher, observing messages with rostopic echo, and confirming rates with rostopic hz. These skills matter because they move you from reading code to verifying live robot behavior. As you practice, pay attention to how message types define fields you can inspect with rosmsg show, and how queue_size affects buffering and stale data.

This second objectives slide focuses on message types, buffering, and practical verification skills you will need in the lab. You will learn to identify standard message types such as std_msgs/String, geometry_msgs/Twist, and sensor_msgs/Image, and to use rosmsg show to inspect their fields. You will practice setting queue_size appropriately so time-sensitive data like images are not processed stale, and you will learn the trade-offs between small queues that always keep recent data and larger queues that buffer commands. Finally, you will run the hands-on activity: a Python integer publisher and a compiled C++ Twist publisher, verifying their rates with rostopic hz and observing messages with rostopic echo. These objectives ensure that you can both author and validate publishers, make informed choices about message types, and interpret rosmsg and rostopic output during debugging sessions.

The publish-subscribe pattern is a one-to-many, asynchronous messaging model where a publisher sends messages to a named topic and subscribers receive them without knowledge of who sent them. In ROS this decoupling is essential: sensors, planners, and controllers interact through topics rather than direct links. The Master coordinates discovery by recording which nodes publish and which nodes subscribe; it does not forward messages. After registration the publisher and subscriber establish direct TCP connections and exchange messages, which keeps the runtime efficient and scalable. A useful mental model is a radio station: the station broadcasts, any number of radios can tune in, and the station doesn't need to track each radio. A common misconception is thinking the Master is in the message path; that is not correct and leads to confusion when diagnosing latency. Another practical point is that topics are asynchronous, so subscribers may receive messages at unpredictable times depending on network and processing load. For example, a camera might stream at thirty frames per second while a processing node subscribes but can only handle five per second; without proper queue sizing the processing node will either lag behind or drop messages. Reflect: which robot data should be broadcast to many consumers and which should be handled point-to-point?

Topics have names like file paths: slashes separate namespaces, and a leading slash indicates a global name. For example /robot/cmd_vel and /camera/image_raw are distinct topics. Names without a leading slash are relative to the node's namespace, which makes it easier to reuse nodes across robots by changing namespaces. Following a hierarchical naming convention helps avoid collisions when multiple robots or sensors are present, and it clarifies intent. A typical convention is to put robot-specific prefixes like /robot1 or /robot2 so tools and launch files can control which robot a node operates on. A common pitfall is assuming a node publishes to the same topic regardless of its namespace; when you move a node under a different namespace its relative topics change. Use absolute names when you want a node to always publish to the same bus, and use relative names when you intend to remap or reuse the node under different namespaces. Think about which naming style will make your system easy to inspect with rostopic list and less error-prone when copying nodes between robots. How Topics Are Named means use hierarchical names and decide between global and relative names to control reuse and prevent collisions.. In practical terms, namespaces, global vs relative names, and common conventions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ROS messages are typed data structures defined in. msg files and compiled into language-specific classes or structs. Typical standard types include std_msgs/String for text, std_msgs/Int64 for integers, geometry_msgs/Twist for velocity commands, and sensor_msgs/Image for camera data. Knowing the structure of a message is essential before publishing or subscribing: you need to know which fields to set or read. Use rosmsg show followed by the message type to print its fields. This lesson focuses on three loop behaviors that determine the reliability of your publisher: publishing rate, queue_size buffering, and clean shutdown. First, the rate: use rospy. Rate or ros::Rate to keep the frequency stable. These objects sleep for the remaining loop time, so short workloads still match the target frequency. Second, queue_size controls how many outgoing messages are buffered if subscribers fall behind. A queue_size of 10 keeps the most recent ten messages; older ones are dropped. For high-rate sensors where only fresh data matters, choose a small queue so your subscriber always processes the latest sample. For command logs where every command matters, increase the queue or consider a service or action. Third, clean shutdown: check rospy. is_shutdown or ros::ok inside the loop so your node stops gracefully on Ctrl+C. A frequent debugging step is to run rostopic hz to confirm the publish frequency and rostopic echo to inspect payloads. When messages are dropped due to a full queue, you will see gaps in subscriber processing or stale data; monitoring hz and bw helps you spot these problems quickly.

The ROS Master is often misunderstood. Its role is discovery: it keeps a registry of nodes and the topics they publish or subscribe to. When a subscriber registers interest in a topic, the Master responds with a list of publisher endpoints and the subscriber establishes direct connections to those endpoints. This direct TCP connection carries the message traffic without going through the Master, which avoids a single bottleneck and increases throughput. Think of the Master as a phone operator that hands out numbers but does not stay on the line. This design also means that once nodes find each other, network topology and firewall rules can affect message flow—if nodes cannot open direct connections, messages will not be delivered even though the Master knows about them. A practical troubleshooting step is to check rostopic info for a topic to see which nodes the Master knows are publishing, and then confirm direct connections at the OS level if you suspect network issues. Queue behavior determines whether subscribers see every message or only recent ones. When a publisher sends messages faster than a subscriber can process, messages accumulate in a queue up to queue_size. If the queue becomes full, older messages are dropped so that the most recent messages are preserved. For time-sensitive data like camera frames, dropping old frames is often desirable because processing an old frame produces stale results; using a small queue or a queue_size of one ensures subscribers process the latest data. For command sequences where each command must be handled, dropping messages is not acceptable and you should either increase the queue or use a different communication mechanism such as services or actions that provide acknowledgements. A practical way to observe queue effects is to run a publisher at a known high rate, subscribe with a slow consumer, and use rostopic echo to see gaps in timestamps. Remember: choosing queue_size is a design decision balancing freshness, memory, and delivery guarantees. Let's summarize the essential ideas. First, the publish-subscribe pattern decouples senders and receivers through named topics; the Master only helps nodes discover each other, and direct TCP connections carry the messages. Second, topics are hierarchical names; use global and relative names intentionally to support reuse and avoid collisions. Third, messages are typed; inspect types with rosmsg show so you know which fields to use. Fourth, authorship patterns in Python and C++ follow similar steps: initialize, advertise or create a Publisher, use a Rate object, loop while not shutting down, and publish messages. Fifth, tools like rostopic list, info, echo, hz, bw, and pub let you inspect, measure, and test topics rapidly. Finally, queue_size determines buffering behavior and trading freshness against guaranteed delivery. Keep these points in mind when you design topic interfaces or debug live robot systems.
